New Mexico's property tax exemption for homeowners is the Head of Family exemption: up to $2,000 of the taxable value of residential property owned by a New Mexico resident head of family (or held in a grantor trust) is exempt.
A nonresident property owner is not entitled to claim the head of family exemption on New Mexico property.
The $2,000 Head of Family exemption has not been adjusted for inflation since 1993, and about 280,000 owners claim it annually.
cite: NM Legislature RSTP handout, Property Tax Overview and Technology (Sept. 2024)

A transferor, transferee, or authorized agent must file a residential property transfer affidavit with the county assessor within thirty days of filing the deed with the county clerk (7-38-12.1).

The affidavit contains names and mailing addresses of transferors and transferees, legal description, full consideration and terms (including seller incentives), and value of included personal property, used only for analytical and statistical purposes.

The affidavit is not required for, among others: a deed from payment in full or forfeiture under a recorded real estate contract; a quitclaim deed to quiet title or clear boundary disputes; a court-ordered conveyance; an instrument from a delinquent tax sale; and an instrument establishing a gift or a distribution from an estate or trust.

A 'small estate' is one worth less than $50,000 that does not include real property; it can be distributed without probate by an Affidavit of Successor in Interest if at least 30 days have passed since death and no probate has been filed.
If the estate includes real property, the personal representative may need to execute a Personal Representative's deed to transfer the property out of the decedent's name.
Probate may be filed in the probate court of the county where the decedent was domiciled, any time between 5 days and 3 years after death; the filing cost is $30.
Probate is not needed for real estate held in joint tenancy or with a recorded Transfer on Death Deed.
A surviving spouse may transfer title to a community property home titled only in the deceased spouse's name by affidavit, filed six months after the death.

If a federal estate tax return is required, the estate's personal representative must also file a return with the Taxation and Revenue Department under the Estate Tax Act (7-7-1 et seq.).
The state estate tax due date is the same as the federal deadline to file and pay, including any extension for the federal return.
Estates and trusts are subject to income tax at personal income tax rates, which is separate from estate tax; estates file the FID-1 and the estate tax return is form RPD-41058.

Electronic recording of real property instruments is governed by 1.11.2 NMAC: filers must enter a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the county clerk to become an authorized filer.

The MOU must require payment of recordation taxes, recording fees or clerk's fees assessed by statute, comply with notarization requirements, and provide a receipt notification including date and time of receipt.
Electronic instruments are rejected if they fail image/file-format specifications, security requirements, New Mexico statute requirements, or the clerk's requirements.

The landlord must first give written notice: a 3-day notice of nonpayment of rent, a 7-day notice of noncompliance, a 3-day notice of substantial violation, or a 30-day notice of termination.
After the notice period expires, the landlord files a Petition by Owner for Restitution with the court, attaching the notices and lease; the filing fee is $77.00.
The service packet must be served on the tenant at least 7 days before the hearing, by someone other than the landlord or landlord's employees.
After eviction the landlord must hold the tenant's left-behind property for three days after the sheriff locks the doors.

If rent is unpaid and the resident fails to pay within three days after written notice, the owner may terminate the rental agreement; tender of the full amount due before the three-day notice expires bars an action for nonpayment.

New Mexico personal income tax starts with federal adjusted gross income, then applies adjustments such as the net capital gains deduction.
For tax year 2025 you may deduct the greater of 100% of net capital gains up to $2,500, or 40% of up to $1,000,000 of net capital gain income.
A spouse filing separately may claim only one-half of the net capital gains deduction allowed on a joint return.
Capital gains and losses from sales of real property located in New Mexico are allocable to this state.

New Mexico is a community property state; property acquired by either or both spouses during marriage is not separate property.
Spouses must use Form 4A-301, the Marital Settlement Agreement, to decide property and debt division; even property already divided must be reported to the court with value.

The divorce is final only when the judge signs the Final Decree of Dissolution of Marriage.

An owner of New Mexico real estate may execute a deed designating a beneficiary who becomes owner on the owner's death; the deed can be revoked or amended at any time without the beneficiary's consent or knowledge.

The deed confers no ownership rights on the beneficiary until the owner dies; at death the beneficiary files a copy of the death certificate with the county clerk where the real estate is located and title passes without probate.
Transfer on death deeds have been available in New Mexico since June 2001 and can only be used for real estate located in New Mexico.
An interest in real property is titled in transfer on death form by recording a deed signed and acknowledged by the record owner (45-6-401).
cite: NM Legislature bill text SB0183 (2010) amending 45-6-401
